summary:
An Allwork.Space report on new Monster survey data covering how perceived overqualification affects hiring outcomes and candidate behavior.

Key findings: 40% of workers believe they lost a job opportunity because an employer judged them overqualified. A further 45% say they have been excited about a role but worried their level of experience would count against them.

Resume editing is widespread. 57% say they would remove experience from their resume if it doubled their odds of being hired, and 43% report already having removed or downplayed part of their background. Older work experience was the most commonly omitted item at 18%. Other elements workers downplay include graduation dates, total years of experience, accomplishments, advanced degrees, leadership experience and senior job titles.

On perceived employer motives, 36% of workers think employers fear an overqualified hire will leave for a better opportunity, and 35% believe employers assume such candidates will demand higher pay. Smaller shares cite employer concerns that experienced candidates will challenge management, fail to fit the team, or get bored.

The piece also notes that applying below one's experience level is often deliberate. Among workers who would knowingly do so, 25% cite better work-life balance as the main reason. Additional motivations include wanting to work for a particular company, reducing stress or responsibility, seeking job stability, finding remote or flexible work, and career change.

The article does not address workplace technology, office operations, hybrid policy or facilities topics; it is focused on labor market and hiring perception dynamics.
